item.text: {"question_id":"5B.8","answer":"During López Obrador’s administration, distributional policy produced material gains for some groups but was not demonstrably fair in actual incidence across classes, regions, genders, and other groups. Federal pension expansion was a ruler-attributed policy: coverage rose from about 5 million older people receiving 580 pesos monthly in 2018 to 10.8 million receiving 2,400 pesos in 2022, and the share of people aged 65 or older receiving a pension at least equal to the income-poverty line rose from 26.0% to 35.2% between 2018 and 2022 (BATCH-0032-E006; BATCH-0054-E004). Associated outcomes included lower poverty and social-security deprivation among older people, but the transfer was not equivalent to comprehensive social-security coverage (BATCH-0032-E004; BATCH-0032-E005). The distribution was nonetheless uneven: the poorest income group’s share of social spending reportedly fell from about 19% in 2018 to 6% in 2020 after targeted programs were replaced or redirected toward universal transfers, while a higher-income group’s share rose; extreme poverty also increased in absolute terms, though the 2022 distribution report was unavailable and pandemic effects were not isolated (BATCH-0012-E016). CONEVAL’s 2018–2022 results show overall poverty falling from 41.9% to 36.3%, but extreme poverty rising from 8.7 to 9.1 million people, social-care deprivation increasing from 16.2% to 39.1%, and the poorest decile experiencing a much greater health-access deprivation rate in 2022 than the richest decile (BATCH-0032-E002; BATCH-0032-E003). The 2023 labor-market improvement—labor poverty falling from 40.1% to 37.3% and real per-capita labor income rising 11.3% between the third quarters of 2022 and 2023—supports short-term gains, but it is not equivalent to full distributional incidence and is not causally assigned to the president (BATCH-0054-E002). Regional outcomes were heterogeneous: 15 of 32 federal entities had higher extreme-poverty levels in 2022 than in 2018 (BATCH-0039-E004). Gender and group disparities persisted: women, especially women in poverty, had lower labor-force participation, lower hourly earnings, less social-security coverage, more unpaid work, and reduced transfer coverage relative to older people and to men; Indigenous women’s share with labor income at least the poverty line was 33.8%, versus 62.8% for non-Indigenous women (BATCH-0048-E013; BATCH-0054-E004). Indigenous and disabled populations also had substantially higher poverty or social-deprivation burdens than the national population (BATCH-0032-E007). Education spending was partly progressive in basic education but disproportionately benefited richer households in higher education and postgraduate education; early-childhood public investment was insufficient, and the 2023 budget did not change the inequitable pattern (BATCH-0048-E001; BATCH-0048-E002). Overall, the evidence supports meaningful but selective and uneven redistribution, not a demonstrated fair distribution of gains and burdens. Most outcome evidence is for 2018–2022 and serves as the baseline entering 2023; 2023 incidence data are incomplete, and federal policy contribution is better supported than exclusive presidential causation.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0032-E006","BATCH-0054-E004","BATCH-0032-E004","BATCH-0032-E005","BATCH-0054-E002"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0012-E016","BATCH-0032-E002","BATCH-0032-E003","BATCH-0039-E004","BATCH-0048-E013","BATCH-0032-E007","BATCH-0048-E001","BATCH-0048-E002","BATCH-0054-E005"],"limitations_and_gaps":["There is no complete 2023 incidence analysis covering taxes, transfers, labor and wage policy, services, investment, and regional distribution together.","Most group, regional, and multidimensional-poverty outcomes end in 2022; the 2023 labor indicators are short-term and do not measure full household incidence.","Program expansion and observed outcomes do not establish exclusive presidential causation; federal, subnational, pandemic, labor-market, demographic, and other external factors remain relevant.","The evidence does not provide a complete gender-disaggregated tax-incidence analysis or a comprehensive comparison of all affected classes and groups.","Some adverse distributional claims, including the poorest group’s reduced spending share, rely on incomplete reporting and figures from 2018–2020 rather than direct 2023 measurement."],"corrections_made":["Recast 2018–2022 adverse indicators as the baseline entering 2023 rather than direct 2023 performance.","Added the direct pension-coverage improvement while distinguishing transfers from comprehensive social-security coverage.","Added regional heterogeneity, gender and Indigenous disparities, and the 33.8% versus 62.8% Indigenous-women income comparison.","Reduced favorable causal weight for labor-income and poverty changes and stated attribution limits explicitly.","Preserved uncertainty around pandemic effects, incomplete incidence measurement, and the unpublished 2022 distribution report."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["A full 2023 tax-transfer-service incidence analysis becomes available.","Verified 2023 gender, Indigenous, disability, regional, and class-disaggregated outcomes materially change the balance.","Evidence clarifies the causal contribution of federal policy versus subnational implementation, pandemic effects, labor-market conditions, or demographic change."]}
